newsitem.title: USA: Colombian Ocampo sees GDP growth as demand revives.
newsitem.headline: Colombian Ocampo sees GDP growth as demand revives.

text.p: The Colombian economy will expand by 3.5 percent in 1996, but build up to 5.0 percent growth next year as domestic demand accelerates, Colombia's Finance Minister Jos Antonio Ocampo said Thursday.

The minister said that domestic demand, which was dampened by high domestic interest rates this year, will lead the economic upswing into next year. Oil and traditional exports will also boost the recovery, he said.
"The government projection is that we will grow at 3.5 percent in 1996," Ocampo said, adding that a private consulting firm pegged this year's growth at 3.1 percent.
The government projects growth of 5.0 percent in 1997 and 6.0 percent in 1998, compared with private forecasts of 4.0 percent and 5.0 percent for the two years, the minister said.

"There is a general consensus the current slowdown will give way to a recovery over the next two years," Ocampo said. "The major driving force in the recovery will be the recovery of domestic demand."
The rebound in neighboring Venezuela should also help the Colombian economy, Ocampo said.

Ocampo, speaking to investors at the Americas Society here, said the strength of the Colombian peso in recent months was due to increased foreign direct investment that brought an increased supply of dollars into the country.
He also linked the peso's strength to the calming of Colombian markets after the easing of the political crisis surrounding President Ernesto Samper.
For much of the year, Samper has been dogged by allegations that he knowingly accepted campaign contributions in 1994 from drug traffickers.
The president, who was exonerated by a Congressional investigation, has steadfastly maintained his innocence and rebuffed numerous calls for his resignation.
Ocampo said that, as the political climate stabilized, market fears of a major peso devaluation dissipated.
He said that the Colombian government stopped bolstering its currency in mid-July, after seeing its mounting strength.
"We stopped selling dollars in mid-July," Ocampo said. "We have not sold a single dollar."
The minister also said the government planned to expand the central government's foreign borrowing to $1.8 billion in 1997 from $1.4 billion this year.
He explained the government's decision earlier this week to postpone a planned mark-denominated bond launch was because of insufficient time to finish the deal.

Ocampo reassured investors on the upcoming rotation of members of the Monetary Board. The terms of two members of the board will expire in February 1997, and the president will appoint their replacements.
"I don't think there should be any major change in monetary stance as a result of the rotation in February 1997," he said.
